artist-002_en.title: Tholu Bommalata
artist-002_en.introduction: Tholu Bommalata ('play of leather figures') is an ancient shadow puppetry tradition of Andhra Pradesh, where intricately chiseled, translucent goatskin puppets are illuminated behind a taut white fabric screen.
artist-002_en.cultural_roots: Originating in the Deccan plateau with documented references dating back over two millennia, the art was fostered by nomadic balladeer communities and royal dynasties including the Kakatiyas and Vijayanagara kings.
materials: Natural mineral and vegetable dyes (madder red
Split bamboo control rods and coir fastenings
techniques: Intricate geometric perforation for light filtration
Multi-jointed limb articulation with bamboo pivots
Translucent back-lit projection with oil lamp illumination
artist-002_en.performance: Performed traditionally across harvest festivals from dusk till dawn, accompanied by harmonium, mridangam, ankle bells (ghungroo), and improvised epic dialogue in Telugu.
artist-002_en.stories_and_traditions: Enacts scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata, interspersed with grassroots humorous interludes reflecting rural agrarian concerns, monsoon forecasts, and ethical satire.
artist-002_en.cultural_significance: Serves as a communal classroom and sacred gathering point, preserving living Telugu dialects, oral musical modes, and visual iconographies through community patronage.
artist-002_en.global_explanation: For audiences encountering this art form for the first time: Tholu Bommalata is kinetic stained-glass theater. Long before electric projection and modern cinema, artisans engineered luminous, articulated storytelling figures whose shadows bridge mortal gatherings with timeless mythology.
artist-002_en.artist_story: Every puppet I shape requires days of silent chiseling. The light carries our village memory through darkness.
sources: Sangeet Natak Akademi Archives on Andhra Folk Arts
Puppetry Traditions of South India (Cultural Heritage Repository)
uncertainties: Exact historical century of transition from animal hides to specialized goatskin parchment remains debated among regional folklorists.
